opus-5.5.text:
Mirror Learning came out of a collaboration led by Jakub Grudzien Kuba. What I found valuable is that it gives you one lens on a whole zoo of algorithms we used to treat as separate things.

Think about where we were. There's classic policy iteration, with nice convergence guarantees. Then there's TRPO, which has a theoretical story, but in practice you make a bunch of approximations and the guarantees get fuzzy. Then there's PPO, which is what everyone actually uses, and the clipping objective was, frankly, a heuristic. It works, but nobody could really tell you why PPO in particular should converge to an optimal policy. There was this awkward gap between what we could prove and what we ran.

Mirror Learning says: here's a general template. You have a drift function, which penalizes how far you move from your current policy. You have a neighbourhood operator, which constrains where you're allowed to move. If those satisfy some fairly mild conditions, you get monotonic improvement and convergence to the optimal policy. And it turns out PPO, TRPO, policy iteration and others are all special cases. So suddenly PPO isn't just a clever hack. It sits inside a space of algorithms that come with guarantees.

The part I'm most excited about is what that buys you. Once you have a theoretically sound space of algorithms, you can search over it. That's what we did in the follow-up work with Chris Lu and others on discovered policy optimisation. We parameterized the drift function, for example with a small neural network, and used meta-learning, essentially evolution, to discover new drift functions that perform well. Because you stay inside the Mirror Learning space, whatever you discover inherits the convergence properties. You're not just doing blind algorithm search and hoping it isn't broken. And the discovered objectives were interesting in their own right. You could look at them, find structure, distill it back into something closed-form and interpretable, and it worked well in practice.

So for me it's a nice example of a broader agenda I care about: use theory not to replace empirical work, but to carve out a safe, expressive space, then let large-scale compute and meta-learning find good things inside it. That's a much healthier relationship between theory and practice than what RL has often had, where theory and practice drift apart and nobody quite knows why things work.

r002.rationale: It identifies PPO’s clipping objective and says PPO is a special case within Mirror Learning, conveying that clipping is one algorithmic choice in the framework.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says the drift function was parameterized with a small neural network.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the thing about Mirror Learning that I found genuinely valuable is that it took something that had been bugging me for years and turned it into a clean mathematical story.

If you look at the practical landscape of deep RL, the algorithms everyone actually uses, PPO, TRPO, and all their relatives, were developed with a kind of mixed motivation. There's a bit of theory, there's a lot of empirical tinkering, and then there's this folklore about why they work. TRPO has a monotonic improvement guarantee in theory, but the thing you actually run is an approximation. PPO was essentially a heuristic simplification of TRPO, with the clipping objective, and the honest story is that it worked well in practice, so people used it, and then the justification got written afterwards. For a long time the field had this gap where the algorithms with the guarantees weren't the algorithms being deployed, and the algorithms being deployed didn't have the guarantees.

What Kuba and the team did with Mirror Learning is show that there's a general family of update rules, defined by a drift function and a neighbourhood operator, and that anything in that family converges to the optimal policy with monotonic improvement. And then it turns out that PPO and TRPO, the actual practical algorithms, not idealised versions of them, are members of that family. So suddenly the thing you run has a guarantee. That was a bit of a revelation, because it means the empirical success wasn't a coincidence. These methods were implicitly satisfying a structure that makes them sound.

The other reason I value it is the flip side of that. Once you have a space of algorithms rather than a handful of named ones, you can start thinking about the space itself. You can ask which drift functions make sense, which neighbourhood operators, and you can even search over that space, which connects to the meta-learning and algorithm discovery work I care a lot about. Instead of hand-designing yet another PPO variant and hoping, you have a principled set of constraints within which you can explore, knowing anything you land on is still well-behaved. It turns algorithm design from a craft into something closer to a design problem with known boundaries.

And then for multi-agent settings, which is where a lot of my interest sits, that framing was especially useful, because it gave us a way to carry those guarantees over to things like HAPPO and HATRPO, where previously you really had no theoretical footing at all when you extended trust region ideas to multiple agents. So it unified a lot, and it opened doors rather than just closing a question.

r001.rationale: It says the framework’s update rules converge to the optimal policy, but does not state the required condition on the penalty for deviating from the data-collecting policy.

r002.rationale: It describes PPO’s clipping objective and says PPO belongs to the framework, but does not identify clipping as one of many possible choices within the framework.

r003.rationale: It discusses exploring drift functions, but does not propose parameterizing a drift function with a neural network and learning it.

astra-6.text:
What I found valuable about Mirror Learning was that it gave us a way to think about what makes a policy update improve performance, without tying ourselves to one particular algorithm. Rather than starting with an objective and hoping that optimizing it does the right thing, you can ask what properties the update needs to have, and then build algorithms within that framework.

It also helps connect approaches that look quite different on the surface. Trust-region methods and PPO-style updates can be understood through a common lens, while leaving room for updates that go beyond standard mirror descent. So for me, the appeal was both explanatory and constructive: it helps us understand existing algorithms, but it also gives us a principled space in which to design new ones.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the value of Mirror Learning was that it gave us a unified way of thinking about policy optimisation. We had algorithms like TRPO and PPO that worked well, but it wasn’t always clear which parts were essential and which were particular design choices.

The framework lets you describe an update in terms of a local objective and a drift function that controls how far you move from the current policy. Under the appropriate conditions, you can establish monotonic improvement and convergence. And the interesting thing is that you don’t have to restrict yourself to the particular form of update you get from mirror descent.

So it becomes a framework for designing algorithms, rather than just analysing an algorithm you already have. You can ask, ‘What other updates satisfy these conditions?’ That opens up a much larger space of possibilities while giving you some theoretical guidance.
